paras: The threatened lynching of William Merriwether took place in Atlanta, Georgia, on the night of September 29, 1888, when a crowd of Black men called for hanging him after he fatally cut Marion Cunningham in an Ivy street billiard saloon. Police kept Merriwether from the crowd, and in November a jury convicted him of murder and fixed his penalty at life on the chain-gang. The New York Sun described the crowd as a mob "determined on lynching him," though other reports treated the case as a killing over cards.

Between seven and eight o'clock that Saturday evening, Jack Ryan's billiard saloon on Ivy street was crowded with Black patrons. Merriwether and Cunningham had been playing five up, a card game in which Cunningham lost money, and Merriwether loudly demanded payment. When Cunningham said he did not have the money and turned away, Merriwether struck him with a raised hand, cutting his throat.

Merriwether ran from the saloon, and several Black men joined the chase. Patrolmen Hudson and Skelton followed and found Cunningham lying in a pool of blood near the street car stables. Three of the pursuers, named by the Constitution as Jack Richardson, Pete Carter and Walter Berry, found Merriwether hiding under a wagon in an alley, pulled him out after a struggle, and turned him over to Hudson.

When Hudson walked his prisoner back into the crowd around the dying man, the Constitution reported, cries of "Hang him! Kill him! Shoot him!" were numerous, and "at one time it looked as though they would carry their threats into execution." Cunningham died on a wagon while Dr. Alley was examining him. As Black men pulled the body through the streets, more than a hundred followed, and when they passed the city prison the air filled with yells of "Let's take him out!"

According to the Sun's dispatch, Chief of Police Conley hurried Merriwether to prison, and the dead man's friends lingered around the jail all night, held in check by the police. Merriwether told police that Cunningham had tried to draw a pistol on him, but no pistol was found on the body. Facing the prospect of a mob, he said he did not want to be mobbed and that if he must hang he wanted it "done by law."

An inquest the same night returned a verdict that the killing was murder. After a trial of several days in the superior court, a jury found Merriwether guilty on November 21 and fixed the penalty at life imprisonment on the chain-gang, and Judge R. H. Clark passed sentence at once. The case was to be carried to the supreme court; no report of the appeal's result appears in the coverage.

The case appeared only in white papers. The Atlanta Constitution gave it the longest treatment, a narrative under "CRIMES AND CRIMINALS" with reconstructed dialogue, the names of officers and pursuers, and the crowd's threats. The Sun ran a shortened version of that narrative under the headline "One Negro Kills Another in a Dispute Over a Game of Cards," calling Merriwether "the assassin" and recasting the pursuit as a mob bent on lynching.

The Savannah Morning News carried brief wire items headed "MURDER AT ATLANTA" and, after the trial, "TO THE CHAIN-GANG FOR LIFE," neither of which mentioned a mob. The Washington Critic reduced the killing to a single line about a quarrel over a gambling debt.

The accounts differ on who pursued Merriwether and why. The Savannah wire and the Constitution describe Black bystanders who caught him and held him for the police, with the threats coming afterward from the crowd. The Sun's dispatch, which closely follows the Constitution's wording, instead says the pursuers were a mob intent on lynching and credits Chief Conley, whom the surviving Constitution text does not mention, with stopping them.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of William Merriwether
bases: A crowd of Black men threatened to hang or kill an arrested Black man for a fatal stabbing, and the Sun described a mob 'determined on lynching him' (A2, A3); no one was lynched.

Merriwether was not killed by the crowd: he was held by police and later tried and convicted in superior court (A3, A5). The crowd's threats ('Hang him! Let's take him out!') were extralegal and framed as punishment for the killing of Cunningham (A2, A3), so the episode is a threatened lynching only.

The killing, chase, capture and arrest are reported independently by the Savannah wire (A1) and the Constitution (A3); the lynching threat rests on the Constitution's account (A3) and the Sun's condensed version of it (A2), and the Savannah report does not mention it (A1).

accounts.label: Savannah wire report
accounts.gist: Several Black men chased Merriwether, caught him and held him until a policeman arrested him; an inquest found murder. No crowd threat is mentioned.

accounts.label: Atlanta Constitution (local)
accounts.gist: Three Black men pulled Merriwether from under a wagon for Patrolman Hudson; when he was brought back, the angry crowd cried 'Hang him! Kill him! Shoot him!', and more than a hundred yelled 'Let's take him out!' at the city prison.

accounts.label: New York Sun dispatch
accounts.gist: 'The mob' pursued Merriwether 'determined on lynching him'; Chief Conley prevented it and hurried him to prison, where the dead man's friends lingered all night, held in check by police.

accounts.label: Merriwether's own account
accounts.gist: He said Cunningham tried to draw a pistol on him and that he was protecting his own life; the paper added that no pistol was found on the dead man.

framing.detail: The Constitution ran the story under 'CRIMES AND CRIMINALS' as a crime narrative with dialogue, calling Merriwether 'the negro' and describing the crowd as 'very mad'.
The Sun headlined it 'One Negro Kills Another in a Dispute Over a Game of Cards', called Merriwether 'the assassin' and 'the murderer', and reported the lynching threat without comment.
The Savannah Morning News ran short wire items, 'MURDER AT ATLANTA' and 'TO THE CHAIN-GANG FOR LIFE', with no mention of a mob.
The Washington Critic gave the killing one line in its news digest.
